meta_description: Test your phone's flashlight right in the browser — no app to install. Check if the rear torch or camera flash works on Android and iPhone, instantly.
h1: Phone Flashlight Test: Check Your Torch Online
subtitle: Not sure if your phone's LED flash still works, or just need extra light in a pinch? Click Start Camera, then Turn Torch On and the Mobile Flash and Torch Test tries to control your rear LED directly from the browser. On phones or browsers where that's not supported — including every iPhone — Open Full-Screen White Light turns your screen into a bright light source instead, and you'll find instructions for testing the flash through your phone's native camera app too.

card.fields_html:
Flash & Torch Test

Starts your rear camera, since torch is only ever exposed on a rear-facing lens

Your camera feed will appear here
Click Start Camera and allow access when your browser asks.

Full-Screen White Light

A screen-brightness alternative when torch control isn't available

Most phones don't let a website control the physical LED flash directly — iOS Safari never exposes it at all, and only some Android browsers do. This turns your whole screen into a bright white light instead, useful as a close-range light source or a substitute for the torch this page can't reach.

Testing the Real Flash

When browser torch control isn't supported

To test the actual LED flash hardware (not just this page's ability to control it), open your phone's native Camera app, switch to video or flashlight mode, and toggle the flash there. If it doesn't light up from the native app either, that points to an actual hardware fault rather than a browser limitation.

content_html:
Your rear camera flash doubles as a flashlight the instant your browser lets a webpage reach it, and this phone flashlight test puts that switch right on the page — no app store detour required. Tap the button, grant access once, and your torch fires live, on the spot. If it stays dark, a bright white screen light here works as a backup, and you'll find the exact reasons a torch button can end up grayed out further down.

How the Phone Flashlight Test Works

Because a webpage needs a live video stream to reach the torch at all, most of these tools quietly open a small preview window even though you only came for the light. That preview is a side effect of the access you already granted, not a separate feature to manage — most people never notice it before the light switches on.

Granting Camera Access

The first tap triggers a permission prompt. If nothing happens after you accept it, the page likely got blocked earlier. Look for a small icon in the address bar and click it to restore webcam access, or open your browser's site settings and flip the permission back to Allow. On Android, you may also need to enable camera access at the OS level — Settings, Apps, your browser, Permissions, Camera, Allow — before the prompt reappears.

What Happens When You Tap the Button

Once access is granted, the page calls the browser's getUserMedia API with a video constraint that asks for the rear-facing lens rather than the selfie camera. A live preview appears, along with whatever resolution and frame rate your camera driver actually negotiated for this device — often lower than the sensor's true spec, since browsers cap video for performance. From there, the page reads the stream's reported capabilities, and if that property shows up, switching it on fires the light. Some versions also let you capture frame as a still photo, a bonus that rides on the same access rather than something the flashlight / torch test itself needs.

Troubleshooting a Camera and Flashlight Test That Fails

If you've ever seen a torch button grayed out and wondered why, the answer is almost always the same: the browser simply doesn't expose that control on this camera or platform. That's standard on any front-facing lens, since front cameras rarely carry a flash to begin with. A "camera in use" message instead means another app or tab already has exclusive access — close video calls or other camera tabs, then reload. If the phone feels sluggish or the battery is critically low, some models disable the light automatically to save power, so it's worth a quick charge before assuming the hardware is at fault.

Camera Permission Denied or Blocked

Denied access is the single most common reason nothing happens. Revisiting the browser's site settings and re-granting the camera permission prompt usually resolves it in one click, and reloading the page afterward lets the request run again from a clean state.

Front Camera Has No Flash LED

Switching to the front lens and expecting light is the second most common dead end — almost no phone builds a flash into the selfie camera, so the button simply has nothing to switch on. Flip back to the rear lens and the test should behave normally, assuming the flash itself is intact.

Confirming the Flash Before a Trade-In Quote

Maria is trading in a two-year-old Pixel 7a through her carrier's buyback program, which grades devices Excellent, Good, Fair, or Poor and cuts the quoted price by roughly 30% if any camera or flash function fails inspection. The trade-in form quotes her $187 for Good condition, but it also asks her to confirm every camera function works before she locks that number in — and she'd rather check than guess, since a failed flash would drop the offer to around $131.

She opens this page directly on the Pixel itself and taps the button. The browser asks for camera access; she allows it, since the request clearly comes from the page she's already on. Within a couple of seconds a live preview replaces the placeholder, reporting a 1280×720 stream at 30 frames per second, and the LED beside the rear lens snaps on at full brightness on the first try — no flicker, no half-second delay. She switches it off, waits a moment, then fires it again to rule out a fluke. Same instant response both times.

With the flash confirmed, Maria works through the rest of the trade-in checklist — screen, speaker, charging port — and submits the form expecting the original $187 quote to hold rather than sliding to the Fair-condition range. The confirmation email lands nine minutes later at the full quoted amount, and she boxes the phone up that same afternoon instead of waiting on a counter-offer or a second inspection request.

Flash Light Alternatives: White Screen and Camera Flash

If your rear LED torch is confirmed dead — no click, no flicker, nothing at all — the flash light options on this page fall back to a white screen light instead: a full-brightness white background bright enough to read by or find a dropped key with. It won't out-throw a real camera flash outdoors, but indoors, at arm's length, it does the job just as well.

When to Reach for the Screen Instead

Use the backup whenever the hardware itself is the problem rather than a permission issue — a phone whose flash has physically failed will never respond to a software toggle, no matter how many times you re-grant access. It also works on devices where the browser never exposed that control in the first place, since the screen doesn't depend on any special capability at all.

Testing Your Online Flashlight on Android and iPhone

This online flashlight behaves a little differently depending on your phone. Bookmark it once and you'll have a flashlight online for either platform, without needing separate apps for each.

Torch Control: Android Chrome vs iOS Safari

Chrome on Android exposes torch control directly, so the button lights up as soon as the rear lens reports it can handle the request. iOS Safari has never implemented that part of the spec, so on an iPhone this page falls back automatically to the white screen light, while the actual torch stays tied to Control Center instead of the webpage.

Everything here runs locally: there's no installation, no uploads, and no account — the video stream and light state never leave your device. That privacy model matters most when you're testing a phone you're about to sell or hand to a repair tech, since nothing gets cached or transmitted in the process.

Treat this flashlight test as a quick self-check, not a full repair diagnosis. If the light, the screen backup, and a restart all fail to bring back any glow whatsoever, that usually points to a genuine hardware fault — a dead flash LED or a damaged flex cable — and needs a proper bench test on a technician's bench rather than another reload.

While you're checking hardware on a smartphone, it's worth running a few other quick diagnostics in the same browser, no installation required:

  • Screen test — fill the display with solid colors right in your browser to spot dead or stuck pixels.
  • Touch test — drag across every zone of the screen to find unresponsive spots.
  • Speaker test and mic test — play tones and watch a live level meter to catch crackle or a dead mic.
  • Sensors test — fire the vibration motor and tilt the device to confirm the gyroscope responds.
  • GPS test — get a live location fix to see how accurately this device reports your position.
  • Charging test — plug in the charger and watch the live battery and charging status flip.
  • Bluetooth test — scan for nearby devices to confirm the radio still works.
  • Face ID or Touch ID — confirm the phone's biometric sensor is present and recognized.
  • Camera test and webcam test — preview the front and rear lenses live to check for blur, spots, or a black frame.

Whenever you need to recheck it — after a software update, before a sale, or just to settle an argument about whether the flash is really dead — it's one tap away, and it never asks you to install anything first.

faq.question: What is a flash and torch test?
faq.answer: A flash and torch test checks whether your device's flash (single burst) or torch (continuous light) is functioning correctly. It evaluates readiness based on brightness level, battery status, duration, and number of cycles to give you a diagnostic score.

faq.question: What is the difference between a flash and a torch?
faq.answer: A flash fires a single, intense burst of light — commonly used in photography for capturing images in low light. A torch (or flashlight mode) keeps the light on continuously for an extended period, useful for illuminating a space.

faq.question: Why is my flash not working on my smartphone?
faq.answer: A flash may fail due to low battery, overheating, software glitches, or hardware damage. Running a flash test helps identify if the issue is related to battery levels or brightness settings before concluding there is a hardware problem.

faq.question: How does battery level affect flash performance?
faq.answer: Flash and torch features draw significant power from your battery. When battery levels drop below 15–20%, many devices automatically disable or limit the flash to protect the battery. Higher brightness levels and longer durations increase battery drain further.

faq.question: What does the readiness score mean?
faq.answer: The readiness score out of 100 reflects how optimal your device's conditions are for running a flash or torch test. It factors in your battery level, brightness setting, test duration, and device type. A score above 70 indicates good conditions for a reliable test.

faq.question: Can using the torch continuously damage my device?
faq.answer: Extended torch use can cause the device to overheat, especially at high brightness levels. Most smartphones have built-in thermal protection that will automatically shut off the torch if the device gets too hot. Keep torch sessions short and at moderate brightness to avoid heat buildup.

faq.question: How many flash cycles should I use for a proper test?
faq.answer: For a standard diagnostic test, 5–10 flash cycles are usually sufficient to verify that the flash fires consistently. If you are testing for photography use, you may want to run more cycles to ensure reliability under repeated use.

faq.question: Does screen brightness affect the torch test result?
faq.answer: The torch operates independently from screen brightness — it uses the camera flash LED, not the display. However, both running at full brightness simultaneously will increase battery drain and heat generation significantly.
